title: Reading (ch. 48)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ora et labora, and the Rule's blunt line that idleness is the enemy of the soul. Your line was pray and work. Did the hinges between your jobs hold? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-eight.

When Lent begins, Saint Benedict's Rule says, each monk is handed a book from the library, and he's to read it straight through, from start to finish. Not skim it. Not sample a chapter and move on. Read the whole thing. It's the same chapter as yesterday, chapter forty-eight, the one that opened by calling idleness the enemy. Yesterday was the work of the hands. But the chapter sets aside other hours, every day, for something just as deliberate. Today: reading.
screen: `IN LENT, A BOOK FROM THE LIBRARY.` → `READ IT STRAIGHT THROUGH.` → `THE OTHER HALF OF CHAPTER 48.`

segments.voice: Benedict's timetable is careful. At certain hours the brothers work with their hands, and at certain hours they're free for holy reading. The hours shift with the seasons, but the reading is always there, set into the day like the prayers are. This is the kind of reading Catholics call lectio divina, holy reading. It isn't reading for information, racing to the end. It's slow. A person reads the scripture or a holy book, stops when a line catches, turns it over, lets it sink, and maybe turns it into prayer. The first psalm describes a person like that, in the Douay-Rheims: "on his law he shall meditate day and night." Benedict knows reading time can go soft. So during the reading hours, he says, one or two senior monks go around the monastery to make sure no brother is idle or chatting, bothering others instead of reading. And on Sunday, everyone is free for reading, except those with duties to do. Then a practical line: if a brother is so careless that he can't or won't read, he's given some work, so that he isn't idle. Even then, the answer is something useful to do, never nothing. What's striking is the respect the Rule gives to reading. It isn't a hobby for the scholarly monks. It's a daily duty for everyone, set at fixed hours, like prayer and work. The hope behind it is that a few lines read slowly, day after day, can reshape a person, the way water shapes a stone.
screen: `SET HOURS FOR HOLY READING.` · `SLOW READING: LECTIO DIVINA.` · `SENIORS CHECK NO ONE IS IDLE.` · `IF HE CAN'T READ, HE'S GIVEN WORK.` · then, large: `ON HIS LAW HE SHALL MEDITATE DAY AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read for fifteen minutes today, slowly, and set it up now. Settle, and breathe. Choose what you'll read: a Gospel passage, a psalm, a page of a saint, or any book that feeds you. Choose when: a set hour, not whenever there's time. Choose where: a chair, a corner, a bench. Now picture yourself there, phone in another room. See yourself reading one line, stopping, and reading it again. No rush to the end of the page. If you pray, you can let the line you stop on become your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Reading. For Benedict, a daily duty at set hours: slow, holy reading, chewed rather than skimmed. Today's word.
Your line: hours for reading. Today, keep the appointment you just made: fifteen minutes, one book, one place, and permission to stop on a single line. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Benedictine communities set aside time each day for lectio divina, the slow, prayerful reading of scripture, and some lay Catholics practice it on their own or in parish groups.

notes: Editor pass: the closing line no longer puts a belief in Benedict's mouth ('Benedict trusts...'); it's framed as the hope behind the practice.

The Rule is paraphrased. Check the summary of ch. 48: set hours for manual labor and lectio divina, varying by season; in Lent each receives a book from the library to read through consecutively; one or two seniors go round during reading to check for idle or chatting brothers; Sunday given to reading except for those with assigned duties; a brother who is negligent or unable or unwilling to read is given work so as not to be idle.
The term 'lectio divina' appears in ch. 48; the description of slow reading that turns to prayer is a general description of the practice, not a quotation from the Rule.
The water-and-stone image is the script's own.
